# C++/WinRT named modules generated by XamlCompiler

Set `<CppWinRTBuildModule>true</CppWinRTBuildModule>` to enable XamlC's named-module output for a C++/WinRT project. The C++/WinRT projection modules used by the project must also be available to the selected MSVC toolset.

The public project module is `<RootNamespace>.Application_Xaml`:

```cpp
import MyApp.Application_Xaml;
```

It is a convenience aggregator over the active XAML class interfaces. A consumer that needs only one XAML declaration can import that class's generated module directly. Importing a XamlC module exposes declarations such as `MainPageT<D>`; it does not define the handwritten `MainPage` implementation or replace C++/WinRT's producer scaffold.

## Generated module graph

Each active XAML class owns an independent declaration interface. The root interface only re-exports those class interfaces. BindingInfo and TypeInfo have their own independent module interfaces; XamlC does not generate a shared Support module or a partition.

For example, when `RootNamespace` and `x:Class` are both `MyApp`-based, a class `MyApp.Views.MainPage` has the logical module name `MyApp.Application_Xaml.Views.MainPage`. Identifiers that are not valid module-name segments, including C++ keywords, are escaped deterministically. Root-level class names `BindingInfo` and `TypeInfo` are also escaped so their modules cannot collide with XamlC's independent BindingInfo and TypeInfo interfaces. These logical names belong to the generated build graph and do not depend on source file paths.

| Output | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `MainPage.xaml.g.h` | A declaration-free sentinel in module mode. It preserves the file C++/WinRT probes while preventing its legacy `TypeT = Type_base` fallback from creating competing XamlC declarations. |
| `MainPage.xaml.g.ixx` | The independent XamlC declaration module for the class. It imports the projection modules needed by the declaration and includes the C++/WinRT `MainPage.g.h` producer scaffold when one exists. |
| `Application_Xaml.g.ixx` | The public root module. It contains only `export import` declarations for the current class modules. |
| `XamlBindingInfo.xaml.g.ixx` | The independent BindingInfo module, when binding support is generated. |
| `XamlTypeInfo.xaml.g.ixx` | The independent TypeInfo module, when TypeInfo is generated. The App class interface re-exports it when the App template needs those declarations. |
| `*.xaml.g.cpp` | Ordinary Pass2 implementation translation units. They import their XamlC modules and include local authored headers after the imports. |
| TypeInfo/provider `.cpp` files | Ordinary translation units as well. They use explicit module imports where needed; the C++/WinRT metadata-provider wrapper remains an ordinary producer source. |

The root module is formed from the project `RootNamespace`; an empty root uses `Application_Xaml`, and an invalid root is encoded beneath `XamlProject`. The class module name is formed from the root plus the class's qualified runtime name, with the root prefix removed when it matches.

## Ordinary implementation translation units

Generated Pass2, BindingInfo, and TypeInfo implementation sources remain ordinary `.cpp` translation units. They do not contain `module;`, `export module`, or `import std;`. Before their first named import, XamlC emits the textual system and STL headers required by that source. The generated preamble then enables the C++/WinRT `WINRT_IMPORT_MODULE` convention and imports `winrt_base`, the required `winrt.<Namespace>` projection modules, and the required XamlC modules.

This ordering gives each translation unit one owner for its standard-library headers. In particular, generated ordinary sources do not import `std` and then textually include STL headers.

The `import std;` preamble is used in actual `.ixx` module interfaces, where the module interface owns that dependency. The generated `.cpp` implementation sources follow the ordinary C++/WinRT 3.x implementation model.

Generated consumers that also need handwritten class declarations include those local headers after their imports. Authored implementation files follow the same C++/WinRT pattern: establish required textual headers first, import the relevant projection and XamlC modules, then include the authored header that includes the ordinary C++/WinRT producer header. The root aggregator is useful when a consumer needs all generated XAML declarations.

`XAML_IMPL_MODULE` scopes XamlC's declaration-producing code in the generated interface. `WINRT_IMPORT_MODULE` is the C++/WinRT producer-header convention used by module-aware consumers. Neither is a project-global build setting, and consumers do not need an XamlC producer/consumer macro.

## Dependency and incremental behavior

XamlC collects declaration dependencies from types, base types, fields, generic arguments, and arrays. Pass2 separately tracks projection dependencies needed by bindings, event hookups, and metadata providers, including external metadata-provider projection namespaces. C++/WinRT remains responsible for its own projection-module dependency graph.

Pass1 records the logical module name for each generated `.ixx` in `GeneratedModuleNames`; MSBuild transfers that name to the compile item and produces its IFC. The module manifest covers the active class interfaces, optional BindingInfo and TypeInfo interfaces, and the root aggregator. Same-leaf XAML files in different directories receive distinct object and dependency paths.

Incremental updates use the complete saved project XAML set, including unchanged classes. Removing, suppressing, or renaming a class removes its interface and manifest entry; MSBuild removes the former IFC and stale source-relative module artifacts. Switching back to header mode removes generated XAML interfaces and IFCs. Content-identical interfaces retain their timestamps.

## Validation

The fork validation PR exercises multi-page and same-leaf namespace fixtures, header/module coexistence, direct per-class and root imports, static-library consumers, incremental graph transitions, the product sample, and a NuGet package consumer. Its full workflow includes formal T4 synchronization, the product build matrix, XamlCompiler tests, and native module consumers. The focused workflow runs the XamlC tests and package/module consumers on the current validation head.

Header mode remains the existing path: it keeps the legacy generated declarations and PCH behavior. Module mode selects its source preamble during generation, so ordinary module-consumer translation units omit the PCH include rather than placing it behind a conditional.
